title: Essential tsconfig options and the strict flags
summary: strict (the default since TypeScript 6.0) is a family of checks; three flags outside it close the holes that bite most often: unchecked index reads, optional properties that may hold undefined, and imports whose fate depends on elision.

examples.title: What strict turns on, and what it catches

annotations.note: verbatimModuleSyntax (TS 5.0): imports without `type` stay in the output, imports with `type` disappear, and nothing in between is guessed. Node's type stripping and esbuild see one file and cannot know that Prefs is only a type, so the rule makes the source say it. It implies isolatedModules.

noImplicitAny is the flag that makes TypeScript a typed language rather than optional hints: a parameter tsc cannot infer must be annotated. Variables and return types are still inferred, so annotate parameters and exported signatures, not every local.

strictNullChecks puts undefined into find()'s return type. Without it, null and undefined are members of every type, which is Java's NullPointerException model. Lesson ts.everyday-types.null goes deeper.
useUnknownInCatchVariables (TS 4.4, part of strict): JavaScript can throw any value, here a string. The cast on line 33 compiles and prints undefined; narrowing with instanceof is the honest version.

examples.title: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and a Turkish lookup key

annotations.note: Record<string, string> promises a string for every key, which no object can keep. Without the flag tsc believes it; the `!` makes that belief visible. "IŞIK".toLowerCase() is "işik" (dotted i), so the lookup misses and the call crashes on undefined.

With the flag (TS 4.1, not part of strict) the read is string | undefined and the compiler forces the miss to be handled. Lowercasing with the "tr" locale maps I to ı and İ to i, which is what Turkish logins need.
Array index reads and destructuring get undefined too. for...of and map() don't, because they only visit elements that exist: prefer them to index loops and the flag costs little.

examples.title: exactOptionalPropertyTypes and the spread that erases a default

annotations.note: Without the flag, `theme?: T` also accepts an explicit undefined. The key then exists ("theme" in loose is true) and object spread copies it, overwriting the default with undefined.
With the flag (TS 4.4, not part of strict), `theme?: T` means absent or a real T. If you really mean "may be present and undefined", write `theme?: T | undefined` and the type says so.

Leaving the key out is the only way to say "not set", so the spread keeps the default. The same distinction matters for PATCH bodies, where a missing field means "don't change" and null means "clear".
JSON.stringify drops undefined properties, so both objects print as {}. Logging the object won't show the bug; the flag catches it at compile time.

use_cases: Starting a project: strict plus noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, verbatimModuleSyntax and erasableSyntaxOnly from day one, when turning them on costs nothing
Tightening an existing codebase one flag at a time: run tsc with the flag on the command line, count the errors, fix, then commit the tsconfig change
Reviewing a pull request that adds `!` or `as` around index reads: each one is a place where the checker was overruled
strengths: Unlike javac's or Go's fixed rules, strictness is adjustable per project, so a JS codebase can be migrated gradually and a new one can start strict
TypeScript 6.0 and 7.0 default strict to true, so a fresh tsconfig already checks null, implicit any and catch variables
noUncheckedIndexedAccess catches the missing-key class of bugs that Java only reports at run time (a null from Map.get) and Go hides behind zero values
weaknesses: The most useful extra flags are not part of strict, so `strict: true` alone still lets arr[i] and record[key] lie
noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds noise to index loops (`for (let i...)` reads are T | undefined even inside bounds); there is no bounds analysis
exactOptionalPropertyTypes trips over library types that write `x?: T` but would accept undefined: passing `{ x: maybe }` then needs a conditional spread or a cast

pitfalls.title: Assuming strict covers index reads
pitfalls.detail: strict does not include noUncheckedIndexedAccess or exactOptionalPropertyTypes. Turn them on explicitly.

pitfalls.title: Silencing the flag with `!` everywhere
pitfalls.detail: A `!` on every index read restores the unchecked behaviour with extra typing. Use for...of, a Map with .get(), or an explicit undefined check that does something sensible.

pitfalls.title: Relying on a missing tsconfig field meaning "off"
pitfalls.detail: Defaults changed in 6.0 (strict, module, target, types). Write the important options explicitly so the file reads the same under every compiler version.

quiz.q: Which flag is NOT turned on by `strict: true`?
quiz.why: noUncheckedIndexedAccess (and exactOptionalPropertyTypes) are separate opt-ins; the other three are members of the strict family.

quiz.q: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, what is the type of `names[0]` when `names: string[]`?
quiz.why: The flag adds undefined to every index-signature and array element read, because the index may be out of range.

quiz.q: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, what happens to `import type { User } from "./user"` in the JavaScript output?
options: It is rewritten to a side-effect import
quiz.why: Imports with the type modifier are erased; imports without it are kept verbatim. That is the whole rule.

body:
## Concept

`tsconfig.json` decides which program you are writing. The same file can be loosely typed
JavaScript or a tightly checked one depending on a handful of flags:

- **`strict`** is an umbrella for the "strict family": `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`,
  `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`,
  `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `noImplicitThis` and `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. New
  members join the family in later releases, so `strict: true` gets stricter when you
  upgrade. **Since TypeScript 6.0 it defaults to true** (also in 7.0). `alwaysStrict`
  went the other way: 6.0 took it out of the family and turned it on unconditionally, so
  `alwaysStrict: false` is deprecated in 6.0 and rejected by 7.0.
- **`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`** (4.1): `arr[i]` and `record[key]` include `undefined`.
- **`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`** (4.4): `x?: T` means "absent or a T", not "or undefined".
- **`verbatimModuleSyntax`** (5.0): imports and exports are emitted exactly as written,
  minus anything marked `type`.

None of the last three is part of `strict`.

This repo's `tsconfig.app.json` is a typical Vite setup: `strict`, `isolatedModules`,
`noEmit` with `allowImportingTsExtensions`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`,
`noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`. It does not turn on the three extra flags. Try them from the
command line without editing anything:
`node node_modules/typescript7/bin/tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json --noUncheckedIndexedAccess`
lists every index read the app takes on trust, such as `lines[i]` in a parsing loop or
`m[1]` from a regex match. Run it for the current count: it changes with the code.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: `javac`'s rules are fixed. TypeScript's are configurable because it had to absorb
  untyped JavaScript gradually. `strictNullChecks` is the switch between Java's model
  (null is in every reference type) and Kotlin's (it isn't, unless you say `T?`).
- C/C++: comparable to `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, except that a TS flag changes what the
  type system believes (`T` vs `T | undefined`), not just which warnings print.
- Python: mypy's `--strict` is the same idea: opt-in checks bundled under one switch.
- Go: the compiler has no strictness knobs; its rules are the same for every module. A
  missing map key gives the zero value; in TS without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` it
  gives `undefined` typed as `T`.
- JS: the flags change nothing at run time. They only change which programs tsc accepts.

## Design notes

For new code, start with everything on: `strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`,
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Each one
turns a whole category of runtime surprise (the missing key, the undefined that overwrote
a default, the import that only existed for types, the enum Node can't strip) into a
compile error, and the cost is lowest on an empty codebase. Tighten an existing project
one flag at a time from the command line, as above, and commit the flag together with
the fixes. Write important options explicitly even when they match today's default: the
6.0 default changes showed that "unset" means different things to different compiler
versions.
